readerTitle: In a five-person agency, culture is last Thursday
caseNote: 가상 사례 (5인 디자인 에이전시, 5인 레스토랑 주방) · 적용 레슨으로 새 개념 없이 '행동으로 드러나는 가치'와 '의식(리추얼)'을 사용
insight: 작은 팀에서는 문화를 만들 필요가 없다. 이미 대표의 매일 결정으로 만들어지고 있으니, 그 결정 몇 개와 작은 반복 습관 하나를 의도적으로 고르면 된다.
misconception: 다섯 명짜리 회사는 문화를 신경 쓸 단계가 아니다. 또는 문화를 만들려면 가치 선언문과 워크숍부터 해야 한다.

sources.text: 모든 인물과 상황은 설명용 가상 예시
이 유닛의 개념 레슨 PPL-06-02 (Values in action), PPL-06-03 (Rituals)

factChecks.note: 모든 사례(에이전시 대표 Maya, 레스토랑 주방)는 가상입니다. 실제 수치나 연구 인용은 없습니다. 게시 전 PPL-06-02, PPL-06-03의 개념 정의 문구와 이 레슨의 요약 표현이 일치하는지 확인하세요.
영업 전 브리핑(lineup)과 직원 식사(staff meal) 같은 주방 관행은 업계에서 흔한 일반적 관행으로만 서술했습니다. 특정 식당이나 셰프의 사례로 쓰지 않았는지 확인하세요.
'Watch out' 카드에서 성장에 따른 문화 변화는 PPL-06-04와 겹치지 않도록 한 문장만 언급했습니다. 편집 시 확장하지 마세요.

cards.title: In a five-person agency, culture is last Thursday
body: Maya runs a small design agency. Five people, one room, one shared calendar.
There's no culture deck. There's what Maya did last Thursday, when a client yelled and a deadline slipped. Everyone saw it. Everyone will copy it.

image.label: Five desks in one small studio, everyone glancing at the founder
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 디자인 스튜디오, 책상 다섯 개. 가운데 대표가 전화 통화 중이고 나머지 네 명이 모니터 너머로 슬쩍 대표를 보고 있음. 실제 로고나 브랜드 없음.

cards.title: Maya wants to "work on culture."
body: Business is steady. Maya notices the team copies her habits, good and bad. She has one afternoon to spend on culture.
What's the best use of it?

options.text: Write a values page with the team and put it on the wall
options.feedback: It starts a useful conversation. But words on a wall don't change much until a real decision shows what they cost. That's **values in action**.

options.text: Pick one value and decide now what it will cost in a real situation
options.feedback: This is **values in action**: a value is real when it guides a hard choice. At five people, the team will see that choice directly.

options.text: Skip it. At five people, culture takes care of itself
options.feedback: You save the afternoon, but culture forms anyway. It just forms from accidents, like how you react on your worst day.

cards.title: One value, one hard call
body: Maya picked a single value: **we tell clients the truth early**. She told the team what it meant in practice. No promising dates they can't hit.

Two weeks later, a big client asked for a full rebrand in three days. The honest answer was six. Maya said six, and the client pushed back. She held the line and offered a smaller first step in three days.
Nobody needed a poster after that. The team had watched the value cost something.

cards.title: At five people, every choice is a signal.
body: In a big company, a leader's choices pass through layers before most people notice. In a five-person agency, there are no layers. People hear the phone call.

That makes **values in action** cheap to teach and easy to break. One honest deadline teaches more than a workshop. One quiet overnight rewrite of a junior's work teaches the opposite, whatever the wall says.

cards.title: Feedback is getting thin.
body: The team now works from home two days a week. Designers share work only when it's finished, so problems show up late.
Maya wants people to show rough work early. Which habit fits a team this size?

options.text: A quarterly offsite with a session on giving feedback
options.feedback: Memorable, but it happens four times a year. A habit you want every week needs a moment that comes every week.

options.text: A 30-minute Friday session where everyone shows one unfinished piece, Maya first
options.feedback: This is a **ritual**: small, regular and tied to a value. Maya going first shows that rough work is safe to share.

options.text: A chat channel where people can post praise for each other
options.feedback: Cheap and friendly. But praise isn't the habit Maya wants, and optional channels often go quiet within weeks.

cards.title: Small, frequent, and led from the front
body: A small team can't afford big programs, and doesn't need them. A good ritual for five people takes minutes, repeats on a fixed rhythm, and points at one value.
Maya's Friday session works because it's predictable and because she shows her own messy drafts. If she skipped her turn, the ritual would teach that rough work is only for juniors.

image.label: Five laptops in a circle showing rough sketches on a Friday
image.brief: 화상회의 화면 분할 이미지. 다섯 칸 중 대표 칸이 첫 번째로 강조되고, 각 화면에 미완성 스케치와 낙서가 보임. 상단에 'Friday · rough work' 라벨. 실제 앱 로고 없음.

cards.title: Small-team culture is fragile in its own way.
body: At five people, culture is mostly the founder's personality. Your blind spots become everyone's rules, and nobody may feel able to say so.
Rituals can also harden. If the Friday session turns into a status meeting, drop it or fix it. And hire number six will shift things more than you expect, which is a topic for another lesson.

cards.title: Now it's a five-person kitchen.
body: A chef-owner runs a small restaurant with four cooks. Her stated value: we never send a plate we wouldn't eat ourselves.
Saturday rush. A plate comes up slightly overcooked. A line cook hesitates, then looks at her. What should she do?

options.text: Send it. The rush matters more tonight
options.feedback: You save two minutes, but the whole kitchen learns the real value is speed. That lesson sticks longer than the rush.

options.text: Remake it, say why out loud, and bring it up at the staff meal after service
options.feedback: **Values in action** in front of everyone, then a **ritual** to turn it into a shared lesson. The cost is two minutes and one ticket running late.

options.text: Remake it quietly and talk to the cook privately next week
options.feedback: The plate is right and the cook isn't embarrassed. But the other three cooks miss what the value looks like under pressure.

cards.title: Small teams don't build culture. They choose it, one visible decision at a time.
body: Concepts used: **values in action** (a value is real when it guides a costly choice) and **rituals** (small, regular habits that keep a value alive).
**Try it today:** pick one value and write down the next hard decision where it will cost you something. Then name one 15-minute weekly habit that supports it.
